chunks: And from him, from a number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Ali ibn Bilal, from Al-Hasan ibn Bassam al-Jammal, from a man who said:

I was with Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) between Mecca and Medina in the month of Sha'ban, and he was fasting. Then we saw the crescent of Ramadan, so he broke his fast. I said to him, 'May I be your ransom, yesterday was from Sha'ban and you were fasting, and today is from Ramadan and you are breaking your fast.' He said, 'That was voluntary (fasting), and we may do what we wish, and this is obligatory (fasting), and we may do only what we are commanded.' The explanation of these two reports is that they should be understood as a form of concession (rukhsah), and that whoever fasts a voluntary fast while traveling is not blameworthy, although breaking the fast is preferable. We said this because both reports are mursal (disconnected chain) and not musnad (connected chain). The earlier reports are musnad and agree with the general reports we mentioned in our book Al-Kabir regarding the prohibition of fasting while traveling, such as their saying: 'Fasting while traveling is not from piety.' So it is as if he broke his fast in the city. And those [general reports] apply to both obligatory and voluntary fasting, and the two preceding reports agree with them, and acting upon them is more worthy and more appropriate.

key_terms.الرُّخۡصَة: Concession or dispensation in Islamic law
key_terms.مُرۡسَل: A hadith with a disconnected chain of narrators
key_terms.مُسۡنَد: A hadith with a connected chain of narrators

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on fasting voluntarily while traveling according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Isfahani clarifies the juristic nuance between voluntary (nafl) and obligatory (fard) fasting while traveling, citing Imam al-Sadiq's practice of breaking his fast upon sighting the Ramadan crescent to demonstrate the shift from personal choice to divine obligation. The text highlights a scholarly reconciliation of seemingly contradictory reports by distinguishing between the permissibility of voluntary fasting as a concession and the preference for breaking it, while noting the weaker chain of transmission (mursal) of this specific report compared to stronger, general prohibitions found in al-Kafi.
